claim: Exposure to early-life adversity (ELA) increases the risk for psychopathologies associated with amygdala-prefrontal cortex (PFC) circuits.
source: Exposure to early-life adversity (ELA) increases the risk for psychopathologies associated with amygdala-prefrontal cortex (PFC) circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the introduction section.

claim: Females are more prone to developing disorders including anxiety and depression following ELA compared to males.
source: Males and females appear to be affected differently by ELA, with females more prone to developing disorders including anxiety and depression (Hammen et al., 2000; Heim et al., 2008; Davis and Pfaff, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ELA in humans leads to life-long changes in connectivity and/or functionality of limbic and cortical regions.
source: Evidence suggests that ELA in humans leads to life-long changes in connectivity and/or functionality of limbic and cortical regions (Choi et al., 2009; VanTieghem and Tottenham, 2018), with consequential deficits in emotion regulation and cognition (Tyrka et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Normative developmental changes in task-based functional connectivity (FC) between amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) are accelerated after ELA.
source: Specifically, Tottenham and colleagues illustrated that normative developmental changes in task-based functional connectivity (FC) between amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) are accelerated after ELA with associated changes in anxiety (Gee et al., 2013a) and are particularly evident in females (Dickie and Armony, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Children institutionalized during the first two years of life in orphanages display precocial development of amygdala-mPFC FC.
source: Indeed, children institutionalized during the first two years of life in orphanages display precocial development of amygdala-mPFC FC, though the anatomical substrates for this accelerated connectivity remain unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from prior research mentioned in the text.

claim: The basolateral amygdala (BLA) sends inputs to the mPFC and modulates anxiety-related behaviors in rats.
source: In rats, the basolateral amygdala (BLA) sends inputs to the mPFC and modulates anxiety-related behaviors (Felix-Ortiz et al., 2016), recall of emotionally salient information (McGaugh, 2004), decision-making (St Onge et al., 2012), and goal-directed behavior (Schoenbaum et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Two subpopulations of BLA neurons project to different regions of the mPFC: projections to the dorsal (prelimbic; PL) region are active during threat-associated fear learning and expression, whereas projections to the ventral (infralimbic; IL) region are active upon extinction of fear.
source: Notably, two subpopulations of BLA neurons project to different regions of the mPFC (Senn et al., 2014): projections to the dorsal (prelimbic; PL) region of the mPFC are active during threat-associated fear learning and expression, whereas projections from the BLA to the ventral (infralimbic; IL) region of the mPFC are active upon extinction of fear, or learning about safety signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In typically developing male rats, BLA innervation of mPFC increases through adolescence.
source: In typically developing male rats, BLA innervation of mPFC increases through adolescence (Cunningham et al., 2002), likely contributing to healthy maturation of threat and safety appraisal.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: BLA-mPFC axonal innervation has not yet been evaluated in females.
source: Notably, BLA-mPFC axonal innervation has not yet been evaluated in females, nor has any study examined the effects of ELA on BLA-derived innervation of PL or IL.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: ELA via chronic stress has been shown to increase BLA-derived glutamatergic release within the PFC, which is associated with increased anxiety-like behavior.
source: ELA via chronic stress has been shown to increase BLA-derived glutamatergic release within the PFC, a finding that can be recapitulated via BLA-PFC stimulation in typical mice and is associated with increased anxiety-like behavior (Lowery-Gionta et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Typically developing females display earlier maturation of the PFC compared to males.
source: Notably, typically developing females display earlier maturation of the PFC (Lenroot et al., 2007; Lenroot and Giedd, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ELA-exposed rats showed precocial maturation of BLA-PFC innervation, with females affected earlier than males.
source: ELA-exposed rats showed precocial maturation of BLA-PFC innervation, with females affected earlier than males.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results section.

claim: ELA disrupted maturation of female rsFC, with enduring relationships between rsFC and anxiety-like behavior.
source: ELA also disrupted maturation of female rsFC, with enduring relationships between rsFC and anxiety-like behavior.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results section.

claim: There were no differences in BLA volume based on sex or rearing condition at PD28, PD38, or PD48.
source: Two-way ANOVA for each age revealed no effects of sex or rearing on BLA volume (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BLA volume significantly increased with age from PD28 to PD48.
source: One-way ANOVA showed a main effect of age (F2,48 = 31.74, p<0.0001). Comparisons revealed increased BLA volume between PD28 and PD38 (p=0.002), PD28 and PD48 (p<0.0001); and PD38 and PD48 (p=0.0002) (Figure 1A; BLA anatomical examples can be seen in Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: There were no significant differences in the percent of BLA filled by the BDA anterograde tracer bolus between ages.
source: One-way ANOVA revealed no effect of percent BLA filled (F2,88 = 3.030, p=0.053; small effect size: partial η2 = 0.06) (Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no relationship between percent BLA filled and total innervation at any age.
source: These revealed no relationship between percent BLA filled and total innervation at any age (PD28: R2(28)=0.064, p=0.178; PD38: R2(27)=0.004, p=0.738; PD48: R2(30)=0.057, p=0.189).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analyses.

claim: There was a main effect of rearing on BLA-PL innervation, with ELA showing increased innervation compared to CON.
source: A three-way ANOVA to determine effects of rearing, sex, and age on BLA-PL innervation revealed a main effect of rearing (F1,79 = 14.294, p<0.0001; partial η2 = 0.153), and a three-way interaction (F2,79 = 5.244, p=0.007; partial η2 = 0.116).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of innervation data.

claim: ELA males showed increased PL innervation at PD38 compared to CON males.
source: Two-way ANOVA of male PL innervation showed a trending age x rearing interaction (F2,42 = 2.748, p=0.076) with a moderate effect size (partial η2 = 0.116); follow-up post-hoc showed an ELA-driven increase in innervation at PD38 compared to CON (p=0.031).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of innervation data.

claim: ELA females showed increased PL innervation at PD28 and PD48 compared to CON females.
source: Two-way ANOVA of female PL innervation showed a main effect of rearing (F1,38 = 14.21, p<0.001; partial η2 = 0.272), with post-hoc indicating more PL innervation in ELA compared to CON at PD28 (p=0.009) and PD48 (p=0.010).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of innervation data.

claim: Male ELA rats showed increased IL innervation from PD28 to PD38.
source: Two-way ANOVA in males showed a main effect of age (F2,40 = 4.355, p=0.019; partial η2 = 0.132), with increased IL innervation from PD28 to PD38 (p=0.015) in ELA.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of innervation data.

claim: Male ELA rats showed more IL2 innervation compared to CON at PD38.
source: In IL2, Males displayed a main effect of age (F2,39 = 4.411, p=0.019; partial η2 = 0.184), and a rearing x age interaction (F2,39 = 4.521, p=0.017; partial η2 = 0.188). Male ELA showed more IL2 innervation compared to CON at PD38 (p=0.007).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of innervation data.

claim: Female ELA rats showed more IL2 innervation than CON at PD28.
source: In females, there was a trending main effect of rearing (F1,38 = 4.791, p=0.035) with a moderate effect size (partial η2 = 0.126), with more IL2 innervation in ELA than CON at PD28 (p=0.037).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of innervation data.

claim: ELA rats overall spent less time in the open arms of the EPM compared to CON rats.
source: Three-way ANOVA comparing time spent in the open arms showed a small effect for a rearing x sex interaction (F2,238 = 4.989; p=0.026; partial η2 = 0.02) as well as a main effect of rearing (F2,238 = 15.833; p=0.004; partial η = 0.04) and of sex (F2,238 = 7.494; p=0.007; partial η2=0.03), with no 3-way interaction (p=0.532; partial η2=0.001) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: ELA females spent less time in the open arms than CON females at PD38.
source: Two-way ANOVAs revealed a main effect in females of rearing (F1,132 = 15.833, p<0.0001; partial η2=0.107), with ELA females spending less time in the open arms than CON at PD38 (p=0.0176).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: At PD28, higher IL innervation in females was correlated with less time spent in the open arms of the EPM.
source: At PD28, higher IL innervation in females was correlated with less time spent in the open arms (R2(14)=0.478; p=0.009) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis presented in Figure 4B.

claim: At PD38, males showed a relationship between less time in the open arms and higher PL innervation.
source: At PD38, males showed a similar relationship between less time in the open arms and higher PL innervation (R2(13)=0.266; p=0.049) (Figure 4C)
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Male CON rats showed stronger BLA-PL connectivity than male ELA rats at PD28.
source: Post-hoc comparisons showed reduced strength of BLA-PL rsFC from PD28 to PD48 in both CON (Z = −3.82) and ELA (Z = −3.26) rats. There was no difference in rsFC between CON and ELA at PD48; however, at PD28 CON showed stronger BLA-PL connectivity than ELA (Z = −4.13; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of rsFC data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Female ELA rats displayed stronger BLA-PL connectivity compared to female CON rats at PD48.
source: Post-hoc showed no difference between CON and ELA at PD28, though a significant difference at PD48 when ELA had stronger BLA-PL connectivity than CON (Z = 4.83; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of rsFC data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Female ELA rats showed less BLA-IL connectivity than female CON rats at PD48.
source: Post-hoc revealed that, at PD48, ELA showed less BLA-IL connectivity than CON (Z = −6.97; Figure 5C), and CON showed increased BLA-IL connectivity from PD28 to PD48 (Z = 4.47), with no significant change seen in ELA.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of rsFC data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Female ELA rats displayed less PD28-PD48 change in BLA-IL rsFC compared to female CON rats.
source: Two-way ANOVA of BLA-IL revealed a moderate effect size for a trend-level sex x rearing interaction (partial η2 = 0.167; F1,25 = 4.09; p=0.054), and post-hoc revealed that females exposed to ELA displayed less PD28-PD48 change compared to CON females (p=0.033) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of rsFC data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: In PD28 females exposed to ELA, lower BLA-IL rsFC predicted less time spent in the open arms of the EPM.
source: Significant correlations revealed that in PD28 females exposed to ELA, lower BLA-IL rsFC predicted less time spent in the open arms (R2(8)=0.852; p=0.001) (Figure 6A)
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis presented in Figure 6A.

claim: In all females, lower BLA-IL rsFC at PD28 predicted less time spent in the open arms twenty days later at PD48.
source: In all females, lower BLA-IL rsFC at PD28 also predicted less time spent in the open arms twenty days later at PD48 (R2(7)=0.405; p=0.011), suggesting an enduring and predictive relationship in females (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis presented in Figure 6B.

claim: In females, lower BLA-IL rsFC at PD48 was associated with less time in the open arms at the same age.
source: This enduring relationship in females was also seen in a significant relationship between lower BLA-IL rsFC at PD48 and less time in the open arms at the same age (Figure 6C; R2(13)=0.303; p=0.041).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis presented in Figure 6C.

claim: This study is the first providing both anatomical and functional evidence for sex- and experience-dependent corticolimbic development.
source: This study is the first providing both anatomical and functional evidence for sex- and experience-dependent corticolimbic development.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract as a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: Pregnant dams were shipped to the facility, therefore all animals in the study underwent shipping stress during gestation.
source: It is important to note here, especially given the current need for more transparency in reporting of ELA paradigms (Kentner et al., 2019; Brenhouse and Bath, 2019) that pregnant dams were shipped to our facility, therefore all animals in our study underwent shipping stress during gestation.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the discussion section.

claim: Effects of maternal separation reported in this study may be a consequence of both prenatal and postnatal stress.
source: It is thus possible that effects of maternal separation reported here are a consequence of both prenatal and postnatal stress, which is common amongst human instances of early life stress (Pedersen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated as a possibility based on the experimental design and supported by a citation.

claim: Females may be particularly vulnerable to neuroanatomical consequences of early adversity, with innervation effects seen earlier in females compared to males.
source: Our findings suggest that females may be particularly vulnerable to neuroanatomical consequences of early adversity, with innervation effects seen earlier in females compared to a later effect observed in males.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: BLA-IL innervation increases through adolescence in a bilaminar manner across development, with more dramatic increases following ELA in both males and females.
source: Our data indicate that BLA-IL innervation increases through adolescence in a bilaminar manner across development, with more dramatic increases following ELA in both males and females.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: Increased innervation to the IL in PD28 females and PD38 males occurred in IL2.
source: Interestingly, increased innervation to the IL in PD28 females and PD38 males occurred in IL2, whereas previous work has shown that in wild-type adult mice, the BLA preferentially targets amygdala-projecting neurons in IL5 over IL2 (Cheriyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: Atypical hyper-innervation after maternal separation may aberrantly target layer 2 of the IL, which may drive the altered maturation of BLA-IL functional connectivity.
source: Since IL2 projection neurons do also project back to the BLA (Gabbott et al., 2005; Little and Carter, 2013), it is possible that atypical hyper-innervation after maternal separation aberrantly targets layer 2, which may drive the altered maturation of BLA-IL functional connectivity we observed in the present work.
evidence: This claim is stated as a possibility in the discussion, supported by citations and inference from the data.

claim: ELA induced BLA-IL innervation that was comparable to more mature (PD48) patterns in female juveniles (PD28) and male early adolescents (PD38).
source: In IL there was evidence of precocial maturation, such that ELA induced BLA-IL innervation that was comparable to more mature (PD48) patterns in female juveniles (PD28) and male early adolescents (PD38).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: Both male and female rats showed an unexpected transient spike in PL innervation that appeared to resolve at the following developmental timepoint.
source: Indeed, within the PL we observed that both male and female rats showed an unexpected transient spike in innervation that appeared to resolve at the following developmental timepoint.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: Reversal of the innervation seen at earlier time points may be due to pruning mechanisms that typically occur in adolescence.
source: It is possible that reversal of the innervation seen at earlier time points may be due to pruning mechanisms (Koss et al., 2014) that typically occur in adolescence, and these mechanisms may serve to mediate excess innervation (Rakic et al., 1994; Spear, 2000; Riccomagno and Kolodkin, 2015).
evidence: This claim is stated as a possibility in the discussion, supported by citations.

claim: The temporary (one week) isolation following surgery may have acted as a secondary stressor acting in conjunction with pubertal changes to produce a resurgence of the ELA-specific phenotype.
source: It is possible that the temporary (one week) isolation following surgery may have acted as a secondary stressor acting in conjunction with pubertal changes to produce a resurgence of this ELA-specific phenotype (Andersen and Teicher, 2008; Tzanoulinou and Sandi, 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated as a possibility in the discussion, supported by citations.

claim: The ages at which ELA-exposed females and males first displayed increased BLA-IL innervation (PD28 and PD38, respectively) were the ages at which higher innervation correlated with higher anxiety-like behavior.
source: Importantly, the ages at which ELA-exposed females and males first displayed increased BLA-IL innervation (PD28 and PD38, respectively) were the ages at which higher innervation correlated with higher anxiety-like behavior (less time spent in open arms of the EPM).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: Monosynaptic input from the BLA to the medial PFC drives aversion to anxiogenic stimuli as measured in the EPM.
source: Since monosynaptic input from the BLA to the medial PFC drives aversion to anxiogenic stimuli as measured in the EPM (Felix-Ortiz et al., 2016), these data suggest that hypertrophic effects of ELA at the BLA-IL circuit lead to heightened anxiety-like behavior in ELA-exposed animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Hypertrophic effects of ELA at the BLA-IL circuit lead to heightened anxiety-like behavior in ELA-exposed animals.
source: Since monosynaptic input from the BLA to the medial PFC drives aversion to anxiogenic stimuli as measured in the EPM (Felix-Ortiz et al., 2016), these data suggest that hypertrophic effects of ELA at the BLA-IL circuit lead to heightened anxiety-like behavior in ELA-exposed animals.
evidence: This claim is stated as a suggestion in the discussion, supported by citation and inference from the data.

claim: Adolescent perturbations have been shown to have lasting consequences on later life function.
source: Transient effects of ELA on innervation and behavior are notable because adolescent perturbations have been shown to have lasting consequences on later life function.
evidence: This claim is supported by general knowledge and citations in the discussion.

claim: Females exposed to ELA displayed dampened maturation of BLA-IL rsFC compared to female CON.
source: Specifically, we report here that females exposed to ELA displayed dampened maturation of BLA-IL rsFC compared to female CON; while no effects of rearing were apparent at PD28, ELA female rats failed to display the increase in BLA-IL rsFC by PD48 that was observed in female CON.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: Increased [more mature] rsFC BLA-IL connectivity in female ELA at PD28 correlated with decreased anxiety-like behavior at that age, as well as 20 days later.
source: Interestingly, increased [more mature] rsFC BLA-IL connectivity in female ELA at PD28 correlated with decreased anxiety-like behavior at that age, as well as 20 days later.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: More mature connectivity in female juveniles may confer enduring behavioral resilience.
source: This suggests that more mature connectivity in female juveniles may confer enduring behavioral resilience, which is consistent with previous reports that dampened connectivity is associated with increased anxiety in adolescence (Kim et al., 2011; Nooner et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is stated as a suggestion in the discussion, supported by inference from the data and citations.

claim: ELA exposure in males resulted in lower juvenile (PD28) rsFC between the BLA and the PL, but no effects on the magnitude of change between PD28-PD48 were noted.
source: While ELA exposure in males appeared to result in lower juvenile (PD28) rsFC between the BLA and the PL, no effects on the magnitude of change between PD28-PD48 were noted, therefore altered maturation per se was not observed in males.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: ELA affected male BLA-PL rsFC at an age that preceded any ELA-attributable increase in innervation, suggesting that the reciprocal connectivity between the two regions was altered without the influence of aberrant amygdalofugal innervation.
source: Interestingly, ELA affected male BLA-PL rsFC at an age that preceded any ELA-attributable increase in innervation, suggesting that the reciprocal connectivity between the two regions was altered without the influence of aberrant amygdalofugal innervation.
evidence: This claim is stated as a suggestion in the discussion, supported by inference from the data.

claim: ELA experience resulted in dampened maturation of BLA-IL rsFC in females, in contrast to the precocial maturation observed in axonal innervation of the IL from the BLA.
source: ELA experience resulted in dampened maturation of BLA-IL rsFC in females, in contrast to the precocial maturation we observed in axonal innervation of the IL from the BLA, as well as the accelerated maturation of task-based FC reported following childhood maltreatment in humans (Gee et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in the results.

claim: BLA-mPFC rsFC in humans has been observed to increase towards more positive connectivity through adolescent development.
source: While BLA-mPFC rsFC in humans has been observed to increase towards more positive connectivity through adolescent development (Gabard-Durnam et al., 2014), task-based FC during fearful face presentations declines from positive connectivity to a negative connectivity (Gee et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Task-based FC between amygdala and mPFC during fearful face presentations was found to reach mature (more negative) levels in previously institutionalized children.
source: This task-based FC was further found to reach mature (more negative) levels in previously institutionalized children (Gee et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Girls who express higher basal cortisol levels at 4.5 years display lower rsFC between the ventromedial PFC and the amygdala at 18 years.
source: In contrast, girls who express higher basal cortisol levels at 4.5 years display lower rsFC between the ventromedial PFC and the amygdala at 18 years (Burghy et al., 2012), corroborating our current findings in PD48 females (see Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: rsFC reflects an intrinsic alternate resonance between different brain areas connected at large scale, in contrast to the more isolated activation of the corresponding brain areas during a task.
source: rsFC reflects an intrinsic alternate resonance between different brain areas connected at large scale, in contrast to the more isolated activation of the corresponding brain areas during a task (Rasero et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Early hyperinnervation to the PFC may alter the stability of the functional BLA-PFC network as it develops, leading to increased anxiety when innervation arises and disrupted maturation of rsFC.
source: Therefore, it appears that early hyperinnervation to the PFC may alter the stability of the functional BLA-PFC network as it develops, leading to increased anxiety when innervation arises and disrupted maturation of rsFC; though how these effects in rats relate to task-based FC is currently unknown.
evidence: This claim is stated as an interpretation in the discussion, supported by inference from the data.

claim: Early maturation of BLA-PFC projections may overwhelm the slow-maturing reciprocal projections to the BLA that dampen anxiety-related circuit activity in mature brains.
source: It is also possible that early maturation of BLA-PFC projections may overwhelm the slow-maturing reciprocal projections to the BLA that dampen anxiety-related circuit activity in mature brains (Arruda-Carvalho et al., 2017; Selleck et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated as a possibility in the discussion, supported by citations.

claim: The present findings support previous work indicating the distinct functional relationship between the BLA and PL and IL regions of mPFC, with PL connectivity related to anxiogenic effects and IL connectivity promoting anxiolytic effects.
source: The present findings support previous work indicating the distinct functional relationship between the BLA and PL and IL regions of mPFC (Calhoon and Tye, 2015), with PL connectivity related to anxiogenic effects (Felix-Ortiz et al., 2016) and IL connectivity promoting anxiolytic effects (Maroun et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and the data presented in the study.

claim: Altered neuroanatomy and functionality of PL and IL, along with BLA, likely have reciprocal effects on one another, further contributing to the exacerbation of ELA-induced anxiety-like phenotypes in adolescence and early adulthood.
source: Furthermore, these findings are in line with the idea that altered neuroanatomy and functionality of PL and IL, along with BLA, likely have reciprocal effects on one another, further contributing to the exacerbation of ELA-induced anxiety-like phenotypes in adolescence and early adulthood (Likhtik and Paz, 2015; Zimmermann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated as an interpretation in the discussion, supported by citations and inference from the data.

claim: Maternal separation in rats was found to disrupt normative development of both anatomical (axonal innervation) and functional (rsFC) connectivity within a circuit regulating emotional processing, with sex-specific effects and evidence of resilience in individuals with precocial maturation of rsFC.
source: Taken together, maternal separation in rats was found to disrupt normative development of both anatomical (axonal innervation) and functional (rsFC) connectivity within a circuit regulating emotional processing, with sex-specific effects and evidence of resilience in individuals with precocial maturation of rsFC.
evidence: This claim is stated as a summary in the discussion, supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: The present findings have implications for intervention based on experience, age, and sex – three functionally interactive factors that uniquely define risk in every individual.
source: The present findings have implications for intervention based on experience, age, and sex – three functionally interactive factors that uniquely define risk in every individual.
evidence: This claim is stated as a conclusion in the discussion.

claim: Timed-pregnant Sprague-Dawley rats arrived at gestational day 15.
source: For Studies 1 (BLA-mPFC innervation) and 2 (rsFC), timed-pregnant Sprague-Dawley rats (Charles River, Wilmington, MA) arrived at gestational day 15.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the methods section.

claim: Rats were housed under standard laboratory conditions in a 12 hr light/dark cycle (lights on at 0700 hr) temperature- and humidity-controlled vivarium with access to food and water ad libitum.
source: Rats were housed under standard laboratory conditions in a 12 hr light/dark cycle (lights on at 0700 hr) temperature- and humidity-controlled vivarium with access to food and water ad libitum.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the methods section.

claim: ELA pups were separated from dams and littermates in individual cups with home cage pine shavings in a circulating water bath (37°C) from PD2-PD10.
source: ELA pups were separated from dams and littermates in individual cups with home cage pine shavings in a circulating water bath (37°C) from PD2-PD10.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the methods section.

claim: At PD11-20, when body temperature is self-regulated, pups were individually separated into cages.
source: At PD11-20, when body temperature is self-regulated, pups were individually separated into cages.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the methods section.

claim: Pups were separated for 4 hr each day (0900 h-1300h) during which time pups were deprived of maternal and littermate tactile stimulation and nursing, but not from maternal odor.
source: Pups were separated for 4 hr each day (0900 h-1300h) during which time pups were deprived of maternal and littermate tactile stimulation and nursing, but not from maternal odor.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the methods section.

claim: 200 nL of BDA was injected into the BLA using a mounted 32-gauge Neuros syringe attached to a microinfusion pump.
source: For maximal uptake without excess bolus, 200 nL (0.2μ l) of BDA was injected into the BLA using a mounted 32-gauge Neuros syringe (Hamilton Company, Reno, NV) attached to a microinfusion pump (11 Elite Nanomite; Harvard Apparatus, Holliston, MA).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the methods section.

claim: BLA-derived axon fiber length was estimated via hemispheric SpaceBalls Probe in four regions per section: PL layer 2 (PL2) and 5 (PL5), and IL layer 2 (IL2) and 5 (IL5).
source: BLA-derived axon fiber length was estimated via hemispheric SpaceBalls Probe in four regions per section: PL layer 2 (PL2) and 5 (PL5), and IL layer 2 (IL2) and 5 (IL5); Figure 1C.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the methods section.

claim: MRI scanning was performed on male and female CON and ELA subjects at PD28 and PD48 in a Bruker BioSpec 7.0T/20 cm USR horizontal magnet.
source: MRI scanning was performed on male and female CON and ELA subjects at PD28 and PD48 in a Bruker BioSpec 7.0T/20 cm USR horizontal magnet (Bruker, Billerica, MA) with a 20 G/cm magnetic field gradient insert (ID = 12 cm) capable of 120µs rise time.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the methods section.

claim: rsFC was measured using seed-based voxel-wise analysis, with BLA as the seeded region.
source: rsFC was measured using seed-based voxel-wise analysis, with BLA as the seeded region.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated in the methods section.
